reference_title: Pavement Design for Roads, Streets, Walks, and Storage Areas

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Soil subgrades support pavements; subgrade strength and uniformity govern required thickness and pavement performance, and moisture/uniformity are especially critical for frost action.
sections.body: Soil subgrades provide a foundation for supporting pavements. The strength and uniformity of the subgrade will affect the required pavement thickness and the performance of the pavement during its design life. Conduct a thorough investigation of the subgrade to determine soil characteristics. Soil uniformity and moisture conditions under the pavement are especially important with respect to frost action.
key_points: Subgrade strength/uniformity directly drive required pavement thickness.
Frost-area design depends heavily on subgrade moisture uniformity.
sections.applicability: Start of every pavement design project -- establishes why a subsurface investigation is required.

sections.title: Investigation of Site
sections.summary: Determine subgrade suitability from classification, moisture-density relationship, compactibility, expansion characteristics, pumping susceptibility, and frost susceptibility; account for groundwater, infiltration, capillarity, topography, and drainage.
sections.body: Characteristics of subgrade soils must be known to predict pavement performance. Determine the general suitability of the subgrade soils based on classification of the soil, moisture-density relationship, degree to which the soil can be compacted, expansion characteristics, susceptibility to pumping, and susceptibility to detrimental frost action. Factors such as groundwater, surface infiltration, soil capillarity, topography, rainfall, and drainage conditions will also affect the future support rendered by the subgrade by increasing its moisture content and thereby reducing its strength.
key_points: Six suitability factors: classification, moisture-density, compactibility, expansion, pumping susceptibility, frost susceptibility.
Environmental factors (groundwater, infiltration, capillarity, drainage) reduce subgrade strength over time by raising moisture content.
sections.applicability: Framing the scope of a subgrade investigation program.

sections.title: Preliminary Site Analysis of Subgrade Conditions
sections.summary: Before field exploration, survey topography/subsurface conditions and at least five years of performance of nearby existing pavements on similar subgrades, using landform, ditch/cut exposures, and published soil/geologic maps.
sections.body: Before planning field explorations, conduct a general survey of the topographic and subsurface soil conditions at the site. Investigate previous performance of existing pavements, minimum of five years, on similar local subgrades to assist in evaluating subsurface conditions. Sources of data should include the landforms, soil conditions in ditches, and cuts and tests of representative soils in the site. Augment the survey with existing soil and geological maps. Sources of information include earlier subsurface investigations near the site, United States Geological Survey maps, and soil survey maps. Evaluate surface drainage at the site and subsurface drainage of the subgrade.
key_points: Review >= 5 years of nearby existing-pavement performance on similar subgrades.
Use USGS maps, soil survey maps, and prior nearby borings to shape the exploration plan.
sections.applicability: Desk-study phase preceding field borings/test pits.

sections.title: Subsurface Explorations
sections.summary: Test each identified soil type via test pits/borings; spacing is 400 ft (120 m) max on uniform subgrades (extendable to 1,500 ft/450 m once confirmed uniform), extending past the frost penetration depth and never less than 6 ft (2 m) below finished grade.
sections.body: Conduct subsurface explorations to test each type of soil identified in the preliminary site analysis. Test pits and soil borings may be used for subsurface investigations. The spacing of subsurface explorations along roadways depends on the variability of the existing soil conditions. When preliminary site analysis substantiates soil uniformity, use a maximum spacing of 400 ft (120 m). Make additional subsurface explorations when the preliminary site analysis indicates unusual or potentially troublesome subgrade conditions. When subsurface explorations have previously been conducted to the required depth and those subsurface explorations confirm soil uniformity, the spacing may be increased to a maximum of 1500 ft (450 m) as long as the subsurface exploration results continue to confirm soil uniformity. The depth of subsurface explorations must extend beyond the frost penetration depth as determined from Chapter titled Seasonal Frost Conditions and be no less than 6 ft (2 m) below finished grade. Depth requirements stated above are measured from the pavement surface.
key_points: Max spacing 400 ft (120 m) generally; up to 1,500 ft (450 m) once soil uniformity is confirmed.
Exploration depth: beyond frost penetration depth AND >= 6 ft (2 m) below finished grade, whichever governs, measured from the pavement surface.
sections.applicability: Planning boring/test-pit spacing and depth for a road or parking-area project.

sections.title: Dynamic Cone Penetrometer
sections.summary: The DCP test (ASTM D6951/D6951M) can be used to determine design CBR values for shallow pavement applications.
sections.body: The Dynamic Cone Penetrometer (DCP) test can be used to determine design California Bearing Ratio (CBR) values. When using the DCP to determine CBR values in shallow pavement applications, perform test in accordance with ASTM D6951/D6951M.
key_points: DCP (ASTM D6951/D6951M) is an accepted design-CBR field method for shallow applications.
sections.applicability: Field CBR estimation where laboratory soaked-CBR testing is impractical.

sections.title: Soil Classification
sections.summary: Classify subsurface exploration samples per the Unified Soil Classification System (ASTM D2487).
sections.body: Classify soil samples from the subsurface explorations according to the Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) in ASTM D2487. This classification is the common language used throughout the rest of this UFC (select material, subbase, base, frost-group, and drainage-material tables are all keyed to USCS symbols).
key_points: All soil classification for this UFC follows ASTM D2487 (USCS).
sections.applicability: Every subsurface sample collected for design.

sections.title: Soil Evaluation
sections.summary: Use exploration samples to compute soil properties, build soil profiles, and select soils for further testing; moisture content evaluation is required to help identify soft layers.
sections.body: Use the subsurface exploration samples to compute soil properties, prepare soil profiles and to select soils for further testing. To help identify soft layers in the soil, evaluations must include moisture content.
key_points: Moisture content evaluation is mandatory -- it is the key indicator of soft/weak layers.
sections.applicability: Converting raw exploration data into a design soil profile.

sections.title: Borrow Areas
sections.summary: Perform preliminary subsurface explorations at borrow sources, extending 2-4 ft (0.6-1.2 m) below the anticipated borrow depth, and classify/moisture-test/compaction-characterize the samples.
sections.body: Perform preliminary subsurface explorations in areas where material is to be borrowed from adjacent areas. Extend subsurface explorations to a minimum depth of 2 to 4 ft (0.6 to 1.2 m) below the anticipated depth of borrow. Use the preliminary samples to classify soils, compute moisture content, and determine compaction characteristics.
key_points: Borrow-area exploration depth: 2-4 ft (0.6-1.2 m) beyond the anticipated borrow depth.
sections.applicability: Qualifying an off-site or adjacent borrow source for select material, subbase, or fill.
